# Socket bayonet (`socket_bayonet`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs handguns_muskets; helped by pike_and_shot_drill
- Core idea: A blade on a sleeve that slips over the muzzle and locks on a stud, with the blade offset to one side so the musket can still be loaded and fired. Every musketeer becomes his own pikeman, the pike disappears, and the whole infantry can both fire and stand against cavalry in thin lines of three or four ranks. The earlier plug bayonet, jammed into the muzzle, stopped the gun firing.
- Pitfalls:
  - Describing the plug type, which blocks the barrel at the moment the enemy charges
  - Barrels and sockets must be made to one size or the bayonets do not fit
  - Thinking bayonets did much killing; their effect was that one side ran before contact
- History: europe: 1640s – plug bayonets in French service (name from Bayonne); 1671 – issued to French fusiliers; 1683 – not yet general, pikes still in use at Vienna; 1687–1689 – Vauban presses for the socket bayonet and France adopts it; 1689 – Killiecrankie, troops with plug bayonets overrun; c. 1700–1705 – pikes abolished in western armies; china: 17th c. – plug bayonets appear in late Ming military manuals
- Read:
  - David Chandler, The Art of Warfare in the Age of Marlborough (1976)
  - John A. Lynn, Giant of the Grand Siècle: The French Army 1610–1715 (1997)
